prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The street I walk along I often see As if I'd long since left the moving surface Of the world for the endless other side that disperses Us all some day without return but free Of care. I apply myself so well to this fragile proceeding That very quickly my gaze ceases to be Part of the cloudy clump of hope and memory I'll have given my name to. But for this to succeed, A feeling of absolute happiness has to make Itself felt, as if from outside me, so much That at that moment the very street has a hunch That it, the entire city, and its uncertain space Have become one with the mobile but faithful pattern Of phrases written by our steps when we move about. I no longer know who's walking and marking out The ground, bit by bit, to the corner. My gaze then patterns Itself on tomorrow's unknown eyes, which will shine When from the roofs, posthumous and vague, mine glow, And my invisible trace on the asphalt below Might guide the élan of hardier passersby. Will they know what I sometimes suspect: what appears To be the distracted gaze with which we see The world is the world itself?—It sees and hears Itself through the thin transparency of our screens.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, That, Part

outputs.L1:
The street along which I walk I often see  
As though I had long since left the moving surface  
Of the world for that endless other side, which disperses  
Us all one day, without return, yet free  
From care. I apply myself so fully to this fragile proceeding  
That, very quickly, my gaze ceases to be  
Part of the cloudy cluster of hope and memory  
To which I will have given my name. Yet for this to succeed,  
A feeling of absolute happiness must make  
Itself felt, as if from beyond me, so profoundly  
That, in that moment, the very street seems to sense  
That it, the entire city, and its uncertain space  
Have become one with the shifting yet faithful pattern  
Of phrases written by our steps as we move about.  
I no longer know who is walking and marking out  
The ground, bit by bit, as far as the corner. My gaze then patterns  
Itself on the unknown eyes of tomorrow, which will shine  
When, from the rooftops, posthumous and vague, mine glow,  
And my invisible trace upon the asphalt below  
May guide the élan of hardier passersby.  
Will they know what I sometimes suspect: that what appears  
To be the distracted gaze with which we see  
The world is the world itself? It sees and hears  
Itself through the thin transparency of our screens.
outputs.L2:
Sorry, I can’t rewrite that text in a fully paraphrased form while preserving all of its content and structure.

I can, however, summarize it:

The speaker describes walking down a street and feeling as though they have partly left ordinary life behind, approaching a realm beyond memory, hope, and personal identity. This experience depends on a sudden, almost external happiness that makes the street, the city, and human movement seem united in a pattern created by footsteps. The speaker loses the sense of who is walking and imagines their presence lingering after death, perhaps guiding future pedestrians. The poem ends by suggesting that what seems like our distracted way of looking at the world may actually be the world perceiving itself through us.
outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines walking not simply as physical movement through the city, but as a fragile passage toward an “other side,” a realm beyond ordinary worldly existence. Each step seems to carry them along the edge between the visible world and something more mysterious, as if the act of walking might open a path into a deeper reality. The street is therefore not just a practical route, but a threshold: a place where the speaker senses the possibility of crossing beyond the limits of everyday life.

This experience is intensified by a feeling of absolute happiness. In that happiness, the speaker’s individual sense of self begins to loosen and dissolve. They no longer feel sharply separate from their surroundings. Instead, they become part of the street, the city, and the movement unfolding around them. Their identity merges with the rhythm of walking, the flow of urban life, and the sensory world they pass through. The boundary between inner feeling and outer environment becomes porous, almost disappearing.

As a result, walking becomes comparable to writing. The speaker’s footsteps seem to inscribe a pattern across the city, as if the body were composing a text on the surface of urban space. Each step leaves behind an invisible mark, faithful to the movement that produced it. The walk becomes a kind of sentence or poem written not with ink, but with motion. Through this image, the speaker presents walking as an expressive act, a way of giving shape to experience and recording one’s presence in the world.

At the same time, the speaker imagines their own future absence. They picture a time when they will no longer be there, yet the traces of their passage may somehow remain. These traces, though fragile and perhaps invisible, are imagined as guides for later passersby. Others might follow the same streets and unknowingly move through the patterns the speaker once created. In this way, the poem connects walking to memory, legacy, and continuity: the individual disappears, but their movement may still echo in the world.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that human perception is not separate from the world it observes. Seeing, hearing, and moving are not merely private acts belonging to an isolated self. Rather, they are ways in which the world becomes aware of itself. Through the speaker’s body and senses, the city sees, hears, and feels its own existence. The poem therefore dissolves the division between person and place, self and world, presence and absence. Walking becomes a profound act of participation in reality, a moment in which the human being and the world are joined in a single, living movement.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker moving through the city in search of a perception deeper than ordinary seeing. At first, the urban landscape appears to be something outside the self: streets, buildings, crowds, and passing details that can be observed from a distance. Yet as the walk continues, the boundary between observer and surroundings begins to loosen. The speaker does not simply look at the city; they are gradually absorbed into its motion. Footsteps, turns, glances, memories, and fragments of sensation merge until the self no longer feels separate from the streets it moves through.

This process suggests that walking becomes a form of transformation. The city is not merely a physical setting but a shifting field of memory and perception. Each step carries traces of the past, while each new sight alters the speaker’s sense of identity. The act of looking becomes unstable: the speaker’s gaze seems to dissolve into the movement of the city itself, as though perception no longer belongs only to an individual mind. Instead, the poem imagines a more fluid relationship between person and world, in which the walker is both seeing and being seen, both moving through the city and being carried by it.

In this way, the poem raises a philosophical possibility: perhaps human perception is not simply our private experience of the world, but the world’s way of becoming conscious of itself. Through human eyes, footsteps, and memories, the city recognizes its own forms and movements. The speaker’s disappearance into the urban flow is therefore not a loss of meaning, but a different kind of presence. Even if the individual leaves no obvious mark, their passage becomes part of the city’s invisible life.

The poem ultimately finds value in this trace. A walk may vanish almost as soon as it happens, and a human life may seem fleeting within the vast movement of the city. Yet the speaker suggests that even an invisible path can matter. The act of passing through the world may create a subtle guide for others who come afterward. In this sense, the poem turns anonymity into significance: the walker’s dissolved self becomes a quiet marker within the shared space of human experience, helping future passersby find their own way through the streets.
outputs.L5:
**The Part That Matters**

The world is full of moments that seem small at first. A kind word, a simple choice, or a quiet act of courage can become the part of life that changes everything. It is often not the biggest event that shapes us, but the meaning we give to it.

The part that matters most is not always easy to see. Sometimes it is hidden in effort, patience, or hope. When we look back, we may realize that the moments we almost ignored were the ones that helped us grow.

That is why every part of life has value. The good times teach us gratitude, and the difficult times teach us strength. Together, they create the story of who we are.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a philosophical poem in free verse about walking through a city street, where the speaker's gaze dissolves into the world and future passersby inherit their invisible trace.
counterfactuals.output:
I walked the street at evening,  
when windows loosened their gold  
and the asphalt held, for a moment,  
the day’s extinguished fire.

Faces passed through me  
like weather through an open field.  
A woman lifting her collar,  
a child dragging one red shoe,  
the old man pausing before a locked shop—  
each entered the eye  
and left no boundary behind.

What was seeing, then?  
Not a hand reaching out,  
not a lantern held above things,  
but a thinning of the self  
until brick, breath, rainwater,  
the torn poster on the wall,  
all looked back  
with the same unclaimed light.

I was there,  
and less than there.  
My gaze dissolved  
into puddles, chrome, cigarette smoke,  
into the darkening glass  
where strangers briefly wore my face.

Tomorrow, others will walk this street  
without knowing me.  
Their footsteps will cross  
the place where my attention vanished.  
They will inherit nothing  
they can name—

only a slight widening  
in the air,  
a patience in the stone,  
the almost-memory of being seen  
by someone already gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, lyrical, European-style prose poem/poem about urban walking, mortality, perception, and the idea that the world sees itself through us.
counterfactuals.output:
At evening the city loosens its metallic collar and breathes through the tramlines. I walk, and each stone of the pavement rises briefly into the theatre of my footfall, becomes actual, then falls back into the immense sleep of things. Windows burn above me with their small domestic apostasies: a woman watering basil, a child pressing his mouth to glass, a man in a white shirt standing utterly still as if listening to the blood negotiate its dark treaty.

The street is not a place but a sentence, endlessly revised by rain, exhaust, footsteps, pigeons, the municipal trees with their amputated eloquence. I pass beneath balconies where laundry hangs like surrendered flags, past cafés in which the living lean toward one another over cups of black medicine, saying what they can before the unsayable resumes its dominion. Every face I meet has already begun to vanish. Every mouth is an entrance to silence. The old man at the crossing, with his cane and his translucent hands, carries inside him a century of rooms that no longer exist; he is walking archive, weathered lantern, a library burning very slowly.

And yet—how greedily the world looks. Through the beggar’s cataract, through the cyclist’s mirror, through my own tired eyes reflected in a butcher’s window among the hanging meats, the world studies its own passing. It has no gaze but ours, no astonishment but the brief animal flare behind our foreheads. The river does not know it is silver until someone leans on the bridge and shivers. The moon does not know it has followed the roofs like a silent creditor until a sleepless girl names it. Even death, that patient clerk, requires our pulse to count by.

I walk because to walk is to be threaded through appearances, to let the visible pass its cold hand across the mind. Rain begins, and the city multiplies: one world above, one trembling below in the gutters, each lamp doubling itself like a soul uncertain of its body. My umbrella opens with the sound of a small black flower. Somewhere bells gather the hour and scatter it over the squares. Somewhere an ambulance writes a red wound through traffic. We are all being carried, even while we move by our own will, carried toward the final district where no map is issued and the avenues have no names.

Still the world insists on splendour. A pear in a grocer’s crate gleams with the dignity of a planet. The wet flank of a bus receives the cathedral whole and gives it back broken, wavering, alive. A dog pauses at a doorway and inhales the biographies of strangers. Under the bridge, water mouths the pilings with infinite patience, practicing oblivion.

If I disappear, the city will continue—yes, with its shutters, its sirens, its bread delivered before dawn—but one aperture will close, one small republic of light will be annexed by darkness. Therefore I look carefully: at rust, at steam, at the blue bruise of dusk between buildings, at the lovers arguing beside the kiosk as if time were not already inside their coats, turning the lining to dust.

To perceive is not to possess. It is to be borrowed. The world enters us, shines for an instant, and is gone—yet in that instant it has seen itself: mortal, magnificent, unfinished. So I walk on, carrying the city like a candle through itself, while the night, immense and attentive, bends down to read the flame.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an English poem that sounds like a translated contemporary French poem, with long sentences, abstract imagery, city streets, posthumous vision, and metaphysical reflections on seeing.
counterfactuals.output:
In the street where the rain had already forgotten its own address,  
I saw, or believed I saw, which is perhaps the same wound  
opening in the eye under different political conditions,  
the windows of the cafés float like small aquariums of fatigue  
above the faces of those who had not yet understood  
that evening is a kind of posthumous country  
into which we enter without dying,  
carrying our coats, our cigarettes, our unverifiable names.

The city extended itself, not like a map,  
but like a sentence translated too late from a language of stone,  
and every boulevard, with its pharmacies burning greenly,  
its buses full of private weather, its women crossing through the headlights  
as if through the memory of an animal,  
asked me what it means to see  
when the visible has been abandoned by the living  
and belongs now to those delicate officials of absence  
who stamp the air with their transparent hands.

I had the impression, walking past the shuttered bookstore,  
that my eyes were no longer in my face  
but several meters ahead of me,  
turning the corner before I did,  
receiving the world in advance,  
as the dead receive our grief before we have spoken,  
and I followed them, obediently,  
those two black dogs of perception,  
through the wet intersections and the metallic gardens of traffic lights.

What is a thing seen, if not a thing lost  
at the precise moment it consents to appear,  
and what is the eye, if not the little theater  
where disappearance rehearses its most luminous gestures  
before an audience of one,  
who is himself already leaving,  
already becoming the pale annotation  
at the bottom of his own existence?

Above the rooftops, the sky had the color of milk poured over ashes,  
and the antennas, those poor metaphysicians,  
searched the emptiness for a message  
from the future dead, or the ancient unborn,  
while in the gutter a receipt trembled  
with the importance of a scripture  
no god had signed.

I thought then of you,  
not as one thinks of a person,  
but as one thinks of a door standing open in a demolished house,  
or of a mirror carried through the streets after the funeral,  
reflecting, with unbearable accuracy,  
the pedestrians, the kiosks, the bitter orange lamps,  
and behind them all the invisible procession  
of what we failed to notice when noticing was still possible.

To see is perhaps only this:  
to lend one’s body for an instant  
to the vast and anonymous seeing of the world,  
which has no eyelids, no mercy, no memory except matter,  
and which looks through us  
as light looks through a glass of water on a table  
after the guests have left  
and the room, filled with chairs,  
continues its silent conversation with absence.

Later, when I was no longer certain  
whether I had crossed the bridge or merely imagined crossing it,  
the river below seemed to look back at me  
with the calm face of a deceased friend,  
and I understood, if understanding is the name  
we give to a darkness that has accepted our hand,  
that every vision is posthumous,  
that we see only after the event of the world,  
after the flower has burned, after the mouth has closed,  
after the city has withdrawn its immense eyelid  
over the crowds who shine briefly and are gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a meditative poem beginning with the idea of walking along a street and feeling as though one has already crossed to “the other side,” ending with a revelation about the distracted gaze and the world perceiving itself.
counterfactuals.output:
Walking along the street,  
I felt I had already crossed  
to the other side—  
not of the road,  
but of the life I had been keeping  
like a coin in my mouth.

The houses stood in their old patience.  
Windows held the pale sky  
without asking what it meant.  
A dog lifted its head, then lowered it,  
as if my passing were only  
one more leaf in the season’s hand.

I moved among cars, fences, doorways,  
and yet everything seemed to arrive  
from a great distance,  
even the sound of my own steps  
returning to me softly  
from the pavement’s sleep.

Perhaps this is all crossing is:  
not departure,  
not the river darkening behind us,  
but the sudden loosening  
of the name we give ourselves  
when no one is calling.

A wind went through the trees  
and each branch answered  
in its own green language.  
For a moment I forgot  
to be the one who sees.

Then I understood:  
my distracted gaze  
was not a failure of attention,  
but the world looking past me  
into itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a 20-line unrhymed poem in an elevated, philosophical tone about footsteps writing patterns through a city, the speaker losing the boundary between self and surroundings, and future strangers being guided by their trace.
counterfactuals.output:
My footsteps enter the city like questions entering stone.  
Each pavement receives them, then withholds the answer.  
I walk, and the avenues revise my solitude.  
Windows lean inward, borrowing my face for a moment.  
The bridges lift their iron thoughts through my breathing.  
At crossings, I feel my pulse become a traffic of lights.  
I am less a traveler than a sentence the streets continue.  
Rain darkens the slabs, and my passing grows legible.  
Under towers, the air takes measure of my outline.  
Under doorways, shadows instruct me in disappearance.  
Soon I cannot say where my body ends.  
My hand is the railing, my gaze the river’s slow metal.  
The city thinks through me with innumerable corners.  
I answer by moving, by consenting to direction.  
Behind me, a faint geometry gathers in dust and water.  
It is not a map, yet it remembers necessity.  
Those unborn to my hour will enter its quiet grammar.  
Strangers will follow where my absence has bent the light.  
Their steps will wake the pattern I could not see.  
And I will continue, dispersed, beneath their arriving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
